idiom_name: authorize(subject, action, resource) decision function plus a guard wrapper on every entry point
implementation_notes: C has no authorization framework, so both halves are hand-written: keep the rules in one decision function (or a small policy or ACL table it consults) and call it from a single guard that wraps every entry point - HTTP route, RPC method, CLI command - so no path evaluates rules itself. The canonical deployment shape in C servers is a request-filter or subrequest hook: nginx's auth_request forwards the request to an authorization subrequest and enforces its 2xx/401/403 result, which is exactly 'centralise the decision, delegate the enforcement'. Return an explicit decision value rather than a bare int, fail closed on a missing policy or lookup error, and take subject attributes from the server-side session instead of request data.
pitfalls: A guard macro that returns from inside the handler is forgotten on one path: an unguarded route is a silent hole because nothing else consults the decision.
Deciding from request data (headers, cookies, a query parameter) that the session never verified makes the decision forgeable; source the subject from server-side state.
Fail-open error handling - a NULL policy table or a failed lookup defaulting to allow - turns a missing rule into access.
